name: Chapter 4: Complex Numbers and Quadratic Equations
description: Complex numbers, algebra, powers of i, modulus and conjugate, Argand plane, polar form, roots of unity and quadratic equations.

cards.term: Why were complex numbers invented?
cards.definition: x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution (x² = −1 is impossible for real x). We extend R so that ax² + bx + c = 0 with D < 0 also has solutions

cards.term: Define i.
cards.definition: i = √−1, so i² = −1. i is a solution of x² + 1 = 0

cards.term: Define a complex number. Real part, imaginary part?
cards.definition: A number z = a + ib with a, b real. Re z = a, Im z = b

cards.term: Trap: for z = 2 + 5i, what is Im z?
cards.definition: 5, not 5i. The imaginary part is the real coefficient of i

cards.term: When are two complex numbers z₁ = a + ib and z₂ = c + id equal?
cards.definition: Iff a = c and b = d: real parts equal AND imaginary parts equal

cards.term: Example 1: 4x + i(3x − y) = 3 + i(−6), x, y real. Find x, y.
cards.definition: Real: 4x = 3 → x = 3/4. Imaginary: 3x − y = −6 → y = 3x + 6 = 9/4 + 6 → x = 3/4, y = 33/4

cards.term: Purely real, purely imaginary, and zero: conditions?
cards.definition: Purely real: b = 0. Purely imaginary: a = 0, b ≠ 0. Zero: a = b = 0 (0 is both)

cards.term: Is R ⊂ C?
cards.definition: Yes: every real a is the complex number a + 0i

cards.term: Trap: is 3 + i > 2 + i meaningful? Is i > 0?
cards.definition: No. Complex numbers are not ordered: z₁ < z₂ makes sense only when both are real

cards.term: How is the complex number x + iy shown geometrically?
cards.definition: As the point P(x, y) of the plane. The plane is the Argand (complex) plane; x-axis = real axis, y-axis = imaginary axis

cards.term: Fig 4.1: read complex numbers off the Argand plane
cards.definition: A=2+4i, B=−2+3i, C=i, D=2, E=−5−2i, F=1−2i: point (x,y) is x+iy; real axis a+0i, imaginary axis 0+bi

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Argand plane · Fig 4.1

Write the complex number represented by each of the points A–F.

x-coordinate → real part, y-coordinate → imaginary part.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Argand plane · Fig 4.1

Write the complex number represented by each of the points A–F.

The point (x, y) is the complex number x + iy:

A = 2 + 4i, B = −2 + 3i, C = i, D = 2, E = −5 − 2i, F = 1 − 2i.

Points on the real axis are a + 0i; points on the imaginary axis are 0 + bi.

cards.term: Which complex numbers lie on the real axis? On the imaginary axis?
cards.definition: Real axis: a + 0i. Imaginary axis: 0 + bi

cards.term: Modulus of x + iy geometrically?
cards.definition: The distance of P(x, y) from the origin: \(|z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\)

cards.term: Conjugate of x + iy geometrically?
cards.definition: The mirror image in the real axis: (x, −y)

cards.term: Add z₁ = a + ib and z₂ = c + id.
cards.definition: (a + c) + i(b + d): add real with real, imaginary with imaginary
−4 + 8i

cards.term: Laws of addition of complex numbers
cards.definition: z₁ + z₂ ∈ C: Closure; z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁: Commutative; (z₁ + z₂) + z₃ = z₁ + (z₂ + z₃): Associative; z + 0 = z: Additive identity: 0 + 0i; z + (−z) = 0: Additive inverse: −a − ib

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

Name the law.

z₁ + z₂ ∈ C?
z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁?
(z₁ + z₂) + z₃ = z₁ + (z₂ + z₃)?
z + 0 = z?
z + (−z) = 0?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
4.3.1 · Laws of addition

Name the law.

z₁ + z₂ ∈ CClosure
z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁Commutative
(z₁ + z₂) + z₃ = z₁ + (z₂ + z₃)Associative

cards.term: Subtraction z₁ − z₂ is defined as?
cards.definition: z₁ + (−z₂). Example: (6 + 3i) − (2 − i) = 4 + 4i, but (2 − i) − (6 + 3i) = −4 − 4i: order matters

cards.term: Addition of complex numbers is vector addition (parallelogram)
cards.definition: z1+z2 is the diagonal of the parallelogram on z1, z2; |z1+z2| ≤ |z1|+|z2| (triangle inequality)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Addition · vector picture

Add z₁ = 3 + i and z₂ = 1 + 2i geometrically.

Slide z₂ so its tail sits on z₁’s tip.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Addition · vector picture

Add z₁ = 3 + i and z₂ = 1 + 2i geometrically.

z₁ + z₂ = (3 + 1) + (1 + 2)i = 4 + 3i: the diagonal of the parallelogram (place z₂ at the tip of z₁).

Hence the triangle inequality: |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂|, with equality only when the two point the same way.

cards.term: Multiply (a + ib)(c + id).
cards.definition:
(ac − bd) + i(ad + bc)
Just expand and use i² = −1
6 + 18i + 10i + 30i² = −24 + 28i

cards.term: Laws of multiplication of complex numbers
cards.definition: z₁z₂ ∈ C: Closure; z₁z₂ = z₂z₁: Commutative; (z₁z₂)z₃ = z₁(z₂z₃): Associative; z · 1 = z: Multiplicative identity 1 + 0i; z · z⁻¹ = 1  (z ≠ 0): Multiplicative inverse; z₁(z₂ + z₃) = z₁z₂ + z₁z₃: Distributive

cards.term: Multiplicative inverse of z = a + ib?
Example 5: multiplicative inverse of 2 − 3i.
Ex 4.1: inverses of 4 − 3i, √5 + 3i and −i.
cards.definition: \(\dfrac{4 + 3i}{25}\), \(\dfrac{\sqrt5 - 3i}{14}\), i (since 1/(−i) = i)

cards.term: Method: how do you divide z₁ by z₂?
cards.definition: Multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator: this makes the denominator the real number |z₂|²

cards.term: Divide (6 + 3i) by (2 − i).
Example 6(i): (5 + √2 i)/(1 − √2 i) in the form a + ib.
cards.definition: Multiply by (1 + √2 i)/(1 + √2 i): numerator 5 + 5√2 i + √2 i − 2 = 3 + 6√2 i; denominator 1 + 2 = 3. Result: 1 + 2√2 i
Numerator 9 + 5 = 14; denominator 2√2 i. \(\dfrac{14}{2\sqrt2\, i} = \dfrac{7}{\sqrt2\, i} = -\dfrac{7}{\sqrt2}\,i\)

cards.term: Ex 2 (i): (−5i)(i/8) in the form a + bi. (ii): (−i)(2i)(−i/8)³?
cards.definition: (i) −5i²/8 = 5/8 + 0i. (ii) (−i)(2i) = 2 and (−i/8)³ = i/512, so i/256

cards.term: Example 3: (5 − 3i)³ = ?

cards.definition: (1 − i)² = 1 − 2i + i² = −2i; square it: (−2i)² = −4
21 + 21i + 7i + 7i² = 14 + 28i

cards.term: Values of i, i², i³, i⁴?
cards.definition: i, −1, −i, 1

cards.term: General formula for integer k?
cards.definition: i⁴ᵏ = 1, i⁴ᵏ⁺¹ = i, i⁴ᵏ⁺² = −1, i⁴ᵏ⁺³ = −i

cards.term: Powers of i cycle every 4 steps
cards.definition: i^n depends only on n mod 4: i^0=1, i^1=i, i^2=−1, i^3=−i; i^43 = −i and i^−35 = i

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Powers of i · intuition

Each multiplication by i moves one step. Find i⁴³ and i⁻³⁵.

Where does 4 quarter-turns bring you?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Powers of i · intuition

Each multiplication by i moves one step. Find i⁴³ and i⁻³⁵.

Each step multiplies by i: a quarter-turn anticlockwise. After 4 steps you are home: i⁴ = 1.

So only the remainder of n ÷ 4 matters: 43 = 4·10 + 3 → i⁴³ = i³ = −i. For −35 = 4·(−9) + 1 → i⁻³⁵ = i¹ = i.

cards.term: Method: how do you evaluate iⁿ for a big or negative n?
cards.definition: Divide n by 4 and keep the remainder (0 to 3). For negative n add a multiple of 4: i⁻³⁵ = i⁻³⁶⁺¹ = i

cards.term: Evaluate i²⁰²³.
cards.definition: 2023 = 4 × 505 + 3 → i³ = −i

cards.term: Evaluate i⁻³⁹ (Ex 4.1 Q3) and i⁹ + i¹⁹ (Q2).
cards.definition: i⁻³⁹: −39 = −40 + 1 → i. i⁹ + i¹⁹ = i + i³ = i − i = 0

cards.term: Example 6(ii): i⁻³⁵ = ?
cards.definition: 1/i³⁵ = 1/(−i) = i (because 1/i = −i)

cards.term: 1/i = ? and 1/i² = ? and 1/i³ = ?
cards.definition: −i, −1, i

cards.term: i + i² + i³ + i⁴ = ? And iⁿ + iⁿ⁺¹ + iⁿ⁺² + iⁿ⁺³?
cards.definition: 0. Any four consecutive powers of i sum to 0 (they go once around the cycle)

cards.term: Sum 1 + i + i² + … + i¹⁰⁰?
cards.definition: 101 terms: the first 100 give 25 blocks of 4, each 0; only the last term i¹⁰⁰ = 1 is left → 1

cards.term: i^n + (1/i)^n: value?
cards.definition: For n = 1: i − i = 0. In general (1/i)ⁿ = (−i)ⁿ, so iⁿ + (−i)ⁿ = 2iⁿ if n even, 0 if n odd

cards.term: Square roots of −1? Of −3?
cards.definition: i and −i. For −3: ±i√3. For a > 0, √(−a) = i√a
No. √−2 · √−3 = (i√2)(i√3) = i²√6 = −√6. The rule √a·√b = √(ab) fails when both a, b < 0

cards.term: When does √a · √b = √(ab)?
cards.definition: When at least one of a, b is non-negative. If both are negative it fails (i² = √(−1)√(−1) ≠ √1)

cards.term: Do the usual identities hold for complex numbers?
cards.definition: Yes: (z₁ ± z₂)² = z₁² ± 2z₁z₂ + z₂², (z₁ ± z₂)³ expansions, and z₁² − z₂² = (z₁ + z₂)(z₁ − z₂)

cards.term: Factorise a² + b² over the complex numbers.
cards.definition: (a + ib)(a − ib): a sum of two squares factorises once i is allowed

2i, −2i, −4, 16
Learn these; they appear constantly.
i, so the n-th power is iⁿ. (Misc Q14: iᵐ = 1 → least m = 4)

cards.term: Define modulus and conjugate of z = a + ib.
cards.definition: |z| = √(a² + b²) (a non-negative real). z̄ = a − ib

cards.term: |2 + 3i|, |2 − 5i|, conjugates of 3 + i, 2 + 5i, 3i − 5?
cards.definition: √13 (= √(4+9)), √29; conjugates: 3 − i, 2 − 5i, −3i − 5

cards.term: Conjugate is the mirror image in the real axis
cards.definition: z̄ reflects z in the real axis; −z is the reflection through the origin; z, z̄, −z, −z̄ all have modulus 5 for z=3+4i

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Conjugate and negative · geometry

Plot z = 3 + 4i, its conjugate z̄, −z and −z̄. What are their moduli?

Reflect in the real axis, then through the origin.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Conjugate and negative · geometry

Plot z = 3 + 4i, its conjugate z̄, −z and −z̄. What are their moduli?

z̄ = mirror image of z in the real axis. −z = reflection through the origin. −z̄ = mirror image in the imaginary axis.

All four lie on the same circle: |z| = |z̄| = |−z| = √(3² + 4²) = 5.

cards.term: z z̄ = ?
cards.definition: |z|²: (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b². A real, non-negative number

cards.term: Two ways to write z⁻¹?
Rules for conjugate and modulus
cards.definition: conjugate of z₁ + z₂: z̄₁ + z̄₂; conjugate of z₁z₂: z̄₁ z̄₂; conjugate of z₁/z₂: z̄₁ / z̄₂  (z₂ ≠ 0); |z₁z₂|: |z₁||z₂|; |z₁/z₂|: |z₁| / |z₂|  (z₂ ≠ 0); conjugate of z̄: z

cards.term: z and its conjugate: tests
cards.definition: z is real: z = z̄; z is purely imaginary: z = −z̄  (z ≠ 0); Re z: (z + z̄)/2; Im z: (z − z̄)/(2i); |z| = 1: z z̄ = 1, i.e. z̄ = 1/z

cards.term: Is |z₁ + z₂| = |z₁| + |z₂|? What is true?
cards.definition: Not in general. |z₁ + z₂| ≤ |z₁| + |z₂| (triangle inequality) and |z₁ − z₂| ≥ ||z₁| − |z₂||

cards.term: Trap: |z|² = z²?
cards.definition: No. |z|² = z z̄, a real number. z² is generally complex: for z = i, |z|² = 1 but z² = −1

cards.term: Example 7: conjugate of (3 − 2i)(2 + 3i)/((1 + 2i)(2 − i)).
cards.definition: Numerator 6 + 9i − 4i + 6 = 12 + 5i; denominator 2 − i + 4i + 2 = 4 + 3i. Divide: \(\dfrac{(12+5i)(4-3i)}{25} = \dfrac{63 - 16i}{25}\). Conjugate: 63/25 + 16/25 i

cards.term: Example 8: x + iy = (a + ib)/(a − ib). Prove x² + y² = 1.
cards.definition: Use moduli: x² + y² = |x + iy|² = |a + ib|² / |a − ib|² = (a² + b²)/(a² + b²) = 1

cards.term: Misc Q1: [i¹⁸ + (1/i)²⁵]³ = ?
cards.definition: i¹⁸ = i² = −1; (1/i)²⁵ = (−i)²⁵ = −i. So (−1 − i)³ = −(1 + i)³ = −(−2 + 2i) = 2 − 2i

cards.term: Misc Q2: prove Re(z₁z₂) = Re z₁ Re z₂ − Im z₁ Im z₂.
cards.definition: With z₁ = a + ib and z₂ = c + id, z₁z₂ = (ac − bd) + i(ad + bc), whose real part is ac − bd ✓

307/442 + (599/442) i
Combine the first bracket over (1−4i)(1+i) first

cards.term: Misc Q5: z₁ = 2 − i, z₂ = 1 + i. Find |(z₁ + z₂ + 1)/(z₁ − z₂ + 1)|.
cards.definition: z₁ + z₂ + 1 = 4, z₁ − z₂ + 1 = 2 − 2i, |2 − 2i| = 2√2. Answer 4/(2√2) = √2

cards.term: Misc Q7: z₁ = 2 − i, z₂ = −2 + i. Find Re(z₁z₂/z̄₁) and Im(1/(z₁z̄₁)).
cards.definition: z₁z₂ = −3 + 4i; divided by 2 + i: (−2 + 11i)/5, so Re = −2/5. z₁z̄₁ = 5 (real), so Im(1/5) = 0

cards.term: Misc Q8: find real x, y if (x − iy)(3 + 5i) = conjugate of (−6 − 24i).
cards.definition: RHS = −6 + 24i. x − iy = (−6 + 24i)/(3 + 5i) = 3 + 3i. So x = 3, y = −3

cards.term: Misc Q9: modulus of (1 + i)/(1 − i) − (1 − i)/(1 + i).
cards.definition: i − (−i) = 2i → modulus 2

cards.term: Misc Q10: (x + iy)³ = u + iv. Show u/x + v/y = 4(x² − y²).
cards.definition: u = x³ − 3xy², v = 3x²y − y³ → u/x = x² − 3y², v/y = 3x² − y²; sum = 4x² − 4y² ✓

cards.term: Misc Q11: |β| = 1, α ≠ β. Find |(β − α)/(1 − ᾱβ)|.
cards.definition: Since ββ̄ = 1: 1 − ᾱβ = β(β̄ − ᾱ) = β · conj(β − α), so modulus = |β||β − α| = |β − α|. The ratio is 1

cards.term: Misc Q12: number of non-zero integral solutions of |1 − i|ˣ = 2ˣ?
cards.definition: |1 − i| = √2, so 2^(x/2) = 2ˣ → x/2 = x → x = 0 only. Non-zero solutions: 0

cards.term: Misc Q13: (a + ib)(c + id)(e + if)(g + ih) = A + iB. Show the product of (a² + b²) etc. is A² + B².
cards.definition: Take moduli: |product| = product of moduli. Squaring: A² + B² = (a² + b²)(c² + d²)(e² + f²)(g² + h²)

cards.term: Misc Q14: ((1 + i)/(1 − i))ᵐ = 1. Least positive integer m?
cards.definition: The base is i, so iᵐ = 1 → m = 4

cards.term: Misc Q4 and Q6: what is the common technique?
cards.definition: Take moduli of both sides: |x − iy|² = |a − ib|/|c − id| etc. Squaring removes the roots, and |a + ib|² = a² + b²

cards.term: Beyond the textbook text (JEE/board): polar form of z = x + iy?
cards.definition: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), with r = |z| = √(x² + y²) and θ = arg z: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ

cards.term: Principal argument: range?
cards.definition: −π < θ ≤ π (Arg z). arg z is defined only up to 2π; z = 0 has no argument

cards.term: Polar form of −1 + i: pick the quadrant first
cards.definition: For z=−1+i: r=√2, θ=3π/4 (second quadrant); tan⁻¹(y/x) alone gives −π/4 (wrong quadrant)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Polar form · argument

Write z = −1 + i in polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ). Which quadrant decides θ?

Sketch the point before computing the angle.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Polar form · argument

Write z = −1 + i in polar form r(cos θ + i sin θ). Which quadrant decides θ?

r = |z| = √((−1)² + 1²) = √2. z is in quadrant II, reference angle tan⁻¹(1/1) = π/4, so θ = π − π/4 = 3π/4.

z = √2 (cos 3π/4 + i sin 3π/4).

Trap: tan⁻¹(y/x) = tan⁻¹(−1) = −π/4 is the wrong quadrant. Always sketch the point first.

cards.term: Trap: arg z = tan⁻¹(y/x) always?
cards.definition: No. tan⁻¹ returns (−π/2, π/2) only. Find the quadrant from the signs of x, y, then use the reference angle: QI θ = α, QII π − α, QIII α − π, QIV −α

cards.term: Multiplication in polar form: |z₁z₂| and arg(z₁z₂)?
cards.definition: |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂|; arg(z₁z₂) = arg z₁ + arg z₂ (mod 2π). Multiplying rotates and scales

cards.term: Division in polar form: |z₁/z₂| and arg(z₁/z₂)?
cards.definition: |z₁|/|z₂| and arg z₁ − arg z₂ (mod 2π)

cards.term: arg(z̄) and arg(−z) in terms of arg z?
cards.definition: arg z̄ = −arg z (mirror in the real axis); arg(−z) = arg z ± π

cards.term: De Moivre’s theorem?
cards.definition:
\((\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta\) for integer n.
Equivalent: (e^{iθ})ⁿ = e^{inθ}

cards.term: Euler’s formula?
cards.definition: \(e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta\). Special case: e^{iπ} + 1 = 0

cards.term: Use De Moivre: (1 + i)⁸ and (1 + i√3)⁶.
Method: raising a complex number to a high power?
cards.definition:
1) Convert to polar r e^{iθ}.
2) Apply rⁿ e^{inθ}.
3) Reduce nθ mod 2π and read off the value

cards.term: Cube root of unity ω: definition and value?
cards.definition: \(\omega = e^{2\pi i/3} = \dfrac{-1 + i\sqrt3}{2}\), the non-real root of z³ = 1

cards.term: Cube roots of unity form an equilateral triangle
cards.definition: z^3=1: roots 1, ω, ω² = (−1±i√3)/2, 120° apart on the unit circle (equilateral triangle)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Cube roots of unity

Solve z³ = 1 and plot the roots.

Factorise z³ − 1 first.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Cube roots of unity

Solve z³ = 1 and plot the roots.

z³ − 1 = (z − 1)(z² + z + 1) = 0 → z = 1 or z = (−1 ± i√3)/2 = ω, ω².

The three roots sit on the unit circle 120° apart: an equilateral triangle. Similarly the n-th roots of unity form a regular n-gon.

cards.term: 1 + ω + ω² = 0 by vector addition
cards.definition: 1+ω+ω²=0 because the three cube roots are equally spaced unit vectors that close a triangle; ω³=1

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Cube roots of unity · sum

Why is 1 + ω + ω² = 0? Add the three roots as vectors head to tail.

Draw 1, then ω from its tip, then ω².
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Cube roots of unity · sum

Why is 1 + ω + ω² = 0? Add the three roots as vectors head to tail.

The three unit vectors at 0°, 120° and 240° form a closed triangle, so they sum to zero.

Algebra: ω satisfies ω² + ω + 1 = 0 and ω³ = 1. So ω² = 1/ω = ω̄ and ω̄ = ω².

cards.term: Properties of cube roots of unity (1)
cards.definition: ω³: 1; 1 + ω + ω²: 0; ω̄: ω² = 1/ω; |ω|: 1; ω²ⁿ or ω³ⁿ⁺¹: reduce the exponent mod 3

ω + ω²?
ω · ω²?
(1 − ω)(1 − ω²)?

Cube roots of unity

Simplify.

1 + ω−ω²
1 + ω²−ω
ω + ω²−1
ω · ω²1
(1 − ω)(1 − ω²)3

cards.term: 1 + ωⁿ + ω²ⁿ = ?
cards.definition: 3 if 3 divides n; 0 otherwise

cards.term: Evaluate ω²⁰²³ and (1 + ω²)³.
cards.definition: 2023 = 3·674 + 1 → ω. And (1 + ω²) = −ω, so (−ω)³ = −ω³ = −1

cards.term: n-th roots of unity: formula, sum and picture?
cards.definition: e^{2πik/n}, k = 0, 1, …, n − 1. Their sum is 0; they are the vertices of a regular n-gon inscribed in the unit circle

cards.term: Locus |z − c| = r is a circle
cards.definition: |z−c|=r is the circle with centre c and radius r; |z−c|<r is its interior; |z−(1+i)|=2 is (x−1)²+(y−1)²=4

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Locus · circle

Describe the set of z with |z − (1 + i)| = 2.

Read |z − c| as “distance from z to c”.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Locus · circle

Describe the set of z with |z − (1 + i)| = 2.

|z − c| is the distance from z to c. So all z at distance 2 from 1 + i: a circle, centre (1, 1), radius 2.

|z − c| < r is the inside, |z − c| > r the outside. Algebra check: (x − 1)² + (y − 1)² = 4.

cards.term: Locus |z − a| = |z − b| is a perpendicular bisector
cards.definition: |z−a|=|z−b| is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining a and b; |z−i|=|z−1| is the line y=x

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Locus · perpendicular bisector

Describe the set of z with |z − i| = |z − 1|.

Equal distances from two fixed points.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Locus · perpendicular bisector

Describe the set of z with |z − i| = |z − 1|.

Points equidistant from i (0, 1) and 1 (1, 0): the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them, the line y = x.

Algebra: x² + (y − 1)² = (x − 1)² + y² ⟹ −2y = −2x ⟹ y = x.

cards.term: What does |z − a| represent geometrically?
cards.definition: The distance between z and a in the Argand plane. |z| is the distance from the origin

cards.term: |z − 2| + |z + 2| = 6 is which curve?
cards.definition: The sum of distances to two fixed points is constant: an ellipse with foci ±2 (Chapter 10)

cards.term: Roots of ax² + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0)?
cards.definition: \(x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\)

cards.term: Discriminant D: definition and the three cases?
cards.definition: D = b² − 4ac. D > 0: two distinct real roots. D = 0: equal real roots. D < 0: two complex conjugate roots

cards.term: Roots when D < 0?
cards.definition: \(x = \dfrac{-b \pm i\sqrt{4ac - b^2}}{2a}\): a conjugate pair

cards.term: Discriminant and x-axis crossings
cards.definition: D>0: two real roots (parabola cuts x-axis twice); D=0: touches once; D<0: no real roots, a complex conjugate pair, e.g. x²−2x+2 has 1±i

cards.term: Solve x² + 1 = 0 and x² + x + 1 = 0.
cards.definition: ±i and (−1 ± i√3)/2 = ω, ω²

cards.term: Solve x² − 2x + 2 = 0.
cards.definition: D = 4 − 8 = −4 → x = (2 ± 2i)/2 = 1 ± i

cards.term: Solve x² + 2x + 5 = 0.
Solve x² − 6x + 25 = 0 and find |root|.
cards.definition: D = 36 − 100 = −64 → x = (6 ± 8i)/2 = 3 ± 4i; each has modulus 5

cards.term: Sum and product of the roots of ax² + bx + c = 0?
cards.definition: \(\alpha + \beta = -\dfrac{b}{a},\qquad \alpha\beta = \dfrac{c}{a}\). Holds for complex roots too

cards.term: Form the quadratic with roots α and β.
cards.definition: \[x^{2} - (\alpha + \beta )x + \alpha \beta = 0\]

cards.term: A real-coefficient quadratic has root 2 + 3i. Find it.
cards.definition: The other root is the conjugate 2 − 3i. Sum 4, product 13 → x² − 4x + 13 = 0

cards.term: Do complex roots of a real polynomial come in pairs?
cards.definition: Yes: if p(z) = 0 with real coefficients then p(z̄) = 0. Similarly irrational roots a + √b come in pairs when the coefficients are rational

cards.term: Fundamental theorem of algebra?
cards.definition: A polynomial of degree n has exactly n roots in C (counted with multiplicity)

cards.term: Solve z² = −4 and z² = i.
cards.definition: z = ±2i. For i: z = ±(1 + i)/√2 (since ((1 + i)/√2)² = 2i/2 = i)

cards.term: Square root of a complex number: method (JEE).
cards.definition: Let (x + iy)² = a + ib → x² − y² = a, 2xy = b, and x² + y² = |a + ib|. Solve the pair for x², y² and choose signs so that xy has the sign of b
±(2 + i) (since (2 + i)² = 3 + 4i) and ±(2 + 3i) (since (2 + 3i)² = −5 + 12i)

cards.term: Trap: x² = −1 has roots ±i. Is √(−1) = ±i?
cards.definition: No. The symbol √−1 means i only (the principal square root); the equation has both ±i

cards.term:
MCQ: The value of i⁵ + i⁶ + i⁷ + i⁸ is
(a) 1 (b) −1 (c) 0 (d) i
cards.definition: (c) 0: four consecutive powers of i

cards.term:
MCQ: (1 + i)/(1 − i) equals
(a) 1 (b) −1 (c) i (d) −i
cards.definition: (c) i: multiply by (1+i)/(1+i): (1+i)²/2 = 2i/2

cards.term:
MCQ: If z = 1 + i, then z² is
(a) 2 (b) 2i (c) −2i (d) 1 + 2i
cards.definition: (b) 2i

cards.term:
MCQ: The conjugate of (2 + i)/(3 − i) is
(a) (1 − i)/2 (b) (1 + i)/2 (c) (5 + 5i)/8 (d) none
cards.definition: Compute (2+i)(3+i)/10 = (6+2i+3i−1)/10 = (5+5i)/10 = (1+i)/2. Conjugate: (a) (1 − i)/2

cards.term:
MCQ: Modulus of (3 + 4i)/(1 − 2i) is
(a) 5 (b) √5 (c) 1 (d) 25

MCQ: If |z| = 1, then z̄ =
(a) z (b) −z (c) 1/z (d) z²
cards.definition: (c) 1/z: z z̄ = |z|² = 1

cards.term:
MCQ: The equation x² + x + 1 = 0 has
(a) real roots (b) complex conjugate roots (c) equal roots (d) imaginary roots only
cards.definition: D = 1 − 4 = −3 < 0 → (b)

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): the least positive integer n with ((1 + i)/(1 − i))ⁿ = 1?
cards.definition: 4 (the base is i)

cards.term: Integer answer: the number of distinct values of iⁿ for integer n?
cards.definition: 4: i, −1, −i, 1

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: √(−2)·√(−3) = √6.
R: √a·√b = √(ab) for all real a, b.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not explain A (c) A true, R false (d) Both false
cards.definition: Both false: √(−2)√(−3) = −√6, and the rule requires at least one of a, b ≥ 0

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: The conjugate of a real number is itself.
R: For z = a + 0i, z̄ = a − 0i = a.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a)

cards.term: True/False (2 marks): if z₁ and z₂ are non-real, then z₁ + z₂ is non-real.
cards.definition: False. z₁ = 1 + i, z₂ = 1 − i: the sum is 2, which is real

cards.term: 3-mark: express (1 + 2i)/(1 − 3i) in the form a + ib and hence find its modulus.
4-mark: if z = x + iy and |z − 1| = |z + 1|, find the locus.
cards.definition: x² − 2x + 1 + y² = x² + 2x + 1 + y² → x = 0: the imaginary axis (perpendicular bisector of −1 and 1)

cards.term: Case-based (AC circuits): impedance Z = 3 + 4i ohm. Find |Z|.
cards.definition: |Z| = √(9 + 16) = 5 Ω. The real part is resistance, the imaginary part reactance; |Z| is the total opposition (Physics 12 link)
